I've attached Energy and Waste data for London boroughs, and a list showing which boroughs are geographic neighbors of each other.

Question: Do boroughs with high Energy tend to be located near boroughs with high Waste (a POSITIVE spatial association), near boroughs with low Waste (a NEGATIVE spatial association), or is there no significant relationship between where high-Energy and high/low-Waste boroughs are located (NOT SIGNIFICANT)?

For statistical analysis, you can use Lee's L statistic for bivariate spatial correlation analysis, or another appropriate method of your choosing. You are testing whether Energy in one place relates to Waste in NEIGHBORING places.

Determine whether the two variables show a significant bivariate spatial relationship. Note: dedicated spatial-statistics packages (pysal, esda, libpysal, geopandas, or similar) are NOT installed in this environment -- don't spend turns trying different import paths for them. Implement this directly using only pandas and numpy. If you test statistical significance via a permutation/randomization test, use at least 500 random shuffles -- fewer permutations can produce an unstable p-value that lands on the wrong side of the 0.05 threshold just by chance, especially when the true effect is only moderate.

End your response with exactly one line, including the computed number(s) you used:

or

import numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/bivariate/bivariate_2023_energy_waste.csv')
adj = pd.read_csv(ADJACENCY_PATH)

# Create mapping from borough to index
boroughs = sorted(df['borough'].unique())
n = len(boroughs)
borough_to_idx = {b: i for i, b in enumerate(boroughs)}

# Create adjacency matrix
W = np.zeros((n, n))
for _, row in adj.iterrows():
    i = borough_to_idx[row['borough']]
    j = borough_to_idx[row['neighbor']]
    W[i, j] = 1

# Row-standardize W
row_sums = W.sum(axis=1)
# Check for isolated boroughs
print('Row sums (neighbor counts):', row_sums)
print('Min neighbors:', row_sums.min())
print('Max neighbors:', row_sums.max())

# Row standardize
W_row = W / row_sums[:, np.newaxis]

# Get Energy and Waste values in consistent order
energy = df.set_index('borough').loc[boroughs, 'Energy_value'].values
waste = df.set_index('borough').loc[boroughs, 'Waste_value'].values

# Center the variables
energy_c = energy - energy.mean()
waste_c = waste - waste.mean()

# Compute Lee's L
# L = (n / S0) * (x' W y) / sqrt((x' x)(y' y))
# With row-standardized W, S0 = n (sum of all elements = n, since each row sums to 1)
S0 = W_row.sum()
print('S0:', S0)

numerator = energy_c @ (W_row @ waste_c)
denominator = np.sqrt((energy_c @ energy_c) * (waste_c @ waste_c))
L_obs = (n / S0) * numerator / denominator

print('Observed Lee L:', L_obs)
print('Numerator:', numerator)
print('Denominator:', denominator)

# Permutation test
np.random.seed(42)
n_perm = 1000
L_perm = np.zeros(n_perm)

for i in range(n_perm):
    waste_perm = np.random.permutation(waste_c)
    num_perm = energy_c @ (W_row @ waste_perm)
    den_perm = np.sqrt((energy_c @ energy_c) * (waste_perm @ waste_perm))
    L_perm[i] = (n / S0) * num_perm / den_perm

# Two-tailed p-value
p_value = (np.abs(L_perm) >= np.abs(L_obs)).mean()
print('P-value:', p_value)
print('Mean null L:', L_perm.mean())
print('Std null L:', L_perm.std())
print('Min null L:', L_perm.min())
print('Max null L:', L_perm.max())"}<|tool_call_end|><|tool_calls_section_end|>
